descriptions.default: A pylon gate stands between the benu heron (the phoenix) and a hawk with a human head, the ba. The deceased claims his dwelling: "The dwelling of Tmu, Lord of Heliopolis, is my dwelling."
A chapter about not letting the man be deprived of his dwelling in the Netherworld.
The deceased stands with a long staff in his hand. The spell lets him who lives in the Netherworld arise and walk unharmed.
A different reading of the title: about not being detrimental to the hour of life in the Netherworld.
A chapter about not letting injure him who is living in the Netherworld.
Jackal-headed Anubis holds up and protects a standing mummy, so that the body does not decay.
A chapter about escaping corruption in the Netherworld.
A tall gate with a ribbed cornice. Through it lies the dark retreat where the shades fall, but the deceased passes and does not die again.
A chapter about not dying again in the Netherworld.
The deceased stands before the gate with a staff in his hand.
A god with a long wig and beard holds two tall sceptres. The deceased adores him so that his head will not be cut off: "They gave me back my head after cutting it off."
The deceased stands with his hands raised in adoration before the god.
A chapter about not letting the man's head be cut off in the Netherworld.
The deceased sits on a chair before an altar heaped with loaves. He refuses filth and lives on bread, wheat and beer from the sycamore of Hathor.
A chapter about not eating any excrement in the Netherworld.
The deceased stands upright, so that he does not go headlong in the Netherworld, where he would have to eat filth.
A chapter about not going headlong in the Netherworld.
A chapter about not entering the place of execution.
The deceased stands near the execution block and keeps away from it.
The block of the place of execution, with a long blade laid across its top. The gods fasten the bones of his neck so that he never comes to it.
The deceased goes out with his staff. The spell repeats chapter 11: he goes out against his foes like Ra rising from the horizon.
A chapter about going out against one's foes in the Netherworld. Its text is the same as chapter 11.
A chapter about going out with the gift of the word being truth. Its text is the same as chapter 10.
The deceased stands ready to go out. The spell repeats chapter 10: he goes out justified, across heaven and earth.
The deceased sits before an altar of loaves and holds out a cup. He drinks nothing foul and eats the loaves of the Lord of offerings. The spell's heading is written above him.
The deceased pours a libation from two bowls before the tall hieroglyph for fire, so that he drinks water and is not dried up by flame. The spell's heading is written above.
A goddess hidden in Nut's sycamore pours water onto the hands of the seated deceased: "O this Nut's sycamore, give me the water which is in thee."
A chapter about drinking water in the Netherworld.
From inside a sycamore, a hidden goddess pours water onto the hands of the bowing deceased and holds out a tray of food.
A chapter about breathing air, about being in possession of the water in the Netherworld.
The deceased carries the sail of breath. He asks for the water as he crosses heaven to the Aarru field.
Another chapter, about being in possession of the water.
The deceased holds up the sail of breath. He comes out of the water and has power over it like the Nile god.
Another chapter, about being in possession of the water.
The deceased raises the sail of breath. He opens the gates of heaven and asks to have the water in his power.
Another chapter of breathing.
The deceased raises the sail of breath and carries an ankh, the sign of life, in his lowered hand. Again he asks Tmu for the breath of his nostrils.
Another chapter whereby air is given.
The deceased holds up the sail of breath. Speaking as Shu, god of the air, he draws breezes from the borders of heaven to the borders of earth.
A chapter about giving air to the man in the Netherworld.
The deceased raises the sail, the hieroglyph for breath. He asks Tmu for the sweet breath of his nostrils.
The deceased holds the sail of breath and a vase. He asks for a door to open, names the parts of his boat, and asks for vases of milk and wine, cakes and meat.
A chapter about breathing air and about being in possession of the water in the Netherworld.
Another chapter, about being in possession of the water.
